v.why: The L2 gradient scales as alpha/batch and is applied n/b times per epoch, so raising alpha at tiny batches drives weight collapse far more than at large batches.
Function change per Adam step grows with fan-in, so wider nets destabilize more at learning rates of 0.08-1 and gain less from width there.
At very high learning rates, larger batches reduce gradient noise and the number of chaotic updates, stabilizing otherwise divergent training.
Large batches leave few updates per epoch, so a higher learning rate compensates for the lost step count.
Large-step errors compound through three ReLU layers, causing dead units and divergence at lower learning rates than in shallow nets.
The L2 penalty shrinks every weight matrix, and the product of shrunken matrices collapses signal multiplicatively in deeper nets.
Extra penalty compounds across three layers of shrunken weights, so increasing alpha costs deep nets more than single-layer nets.
Stacking narrow 16-40 unit ReLU layers creates information bottlenecks and dead-unit cascades, so extra depth hurts there.
With one hidden layer, width is the only source of capacity, so widening helps most there.
Large batches give few updates, and wider nets make more function-space progress per step, so width offsets the reduced step budget.
